title: The importance of change work in schools
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart applies his Run / Serve / Change model of work to inclusion, arguing that inclusion is where the absence of Change work shows most clearly. He contends that most inclusion pressure is caused neither by weak day-to-day practice nor by inadequate support systems but by structural decisions that were never made and have 'leaked downward into people'. Hart defines Change work as architectural: redesigning boundaries, thresholds and where judgement lives, as opposed to conventional improvement initiatives that act within existing structures. He shows how, without it, teachers improvise thresholds, SENDCOs become moral buffers, senior leaders arbitrate case by case and parents escalate. The post offers a diagnostic for inclusion leaders and five sets of Change decisions they are accountable for, from setting inclusion boundaries to fixing thresholds once and legitimising discretion. His conclusion is that strong inclusion leadership is a design discipline, not heroic advocacy.
points: Hart distinguishes Change work from school improvement: improvement acts within existing structures, while Change work redesigns the structures themselves.
He reframes an exhausted inclusion team as carrying 'architectural load' rather than having a resilience problem.
When Change work is missing, Serve systems grow heavier, more procedural and more brittle as they try to compensate.
The predictable failure pattern he names is decisions renegotiated repeatedly, escalation replacing clarity, and leaders permanently busy while nothing stabilises.
Leaders are asked to fix thresholds once and to decide where discretion is legitimate and stand behind it, or 'escalation will always win'.
quotes: Senior leaders can be pulled into endless meetings, mediating the same tensions again and again. Parents can escalate concerns not because they are unreasonable, but because the system has left ambiguity sitting in human relationships.

Change work is architectural. It decides where judgement lives, how risk is carried and which problems the system will stop manufacturing. While improvement work acts within existing structures, Change work redesigns the structures themselves.
An exhausted inclusion team doesn’t have a resilience problem. It is carrying architectural load it was never meant to hold.
Good Serve work does not make Run work easier by offering help. It relocates judgement out of Run altogether, so teachers are no longer asked to decide things the system should have settled already.
Strong inclusion leadership is not heroic advocacy or perfect empathy. It is the discipline of deciding what the system will carry and what it will no longer ask people to absorb.
Most inclusion pressure is not caused by weak Run work and it might not even be caused by not having enough people to do the Run work well. And much of it is not a Serve problem either.
